title: Work by a Constant Force
short: W = Fd cos θ, and a force at right angles to the motion does no work.
trouble: Students think every force on a moving object does work, including the normal force on a level road.

blocks.html: In Work work was force times distance. That holds when the force points along the motion. When it points at an angle, only part of it, its component along the motion, does work.

The work done by a constant force is $\role[work]{energy}{W} = \role{force}{F}\role[displacement]{position}{d}\cos\role[angle between force and displacement]{angle}{\theta}$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Work is in joules ($1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$) and can be positive, negative or zero.

Work measures how much a force adds to (or takes from) an object's energy of motion. A force helps the motion only through its part along the motion, $F\cos\theta$. If the force points backward ($\theta = 180^\circ$, like friction), it takes energy away: negative work. If it is perpendicular ($\theta = 90^\circ$), it neither helps nor hinders: zero work, however hard it pushes.

blocks.name: ph-fbd
blocks.cap: A sled pulled at 30°: only the horizontal part of the pull does work as the sled moves sideways. The normal force and gravity do none.

blocks.title: A pull at an angle
blocks.q: A rope pulls a sled $15\ \text{m}$ across level snow with $70\ \text{N}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. How much work does the rope do?

blocks.title: Work by friction
blocks.q: Friction of $40\ \text{N}$ acts on a box as it slides $6\ \text{m}$. How much work does friction do?
steps: Friction points opposite to the motion: $\theta = 180^\circ$.

blocks.title: Work by gravity
blocks.q: A $5\ \text{kg}$ box is lifted $2\ \text{m}$. How much work does gravity do on it?
steps: Gravity, $49\ \text{N}$, points down; the box moves up: $\theta = 180^\circ$.

blocks.html: Thinking every force on a moving object does work. The normal force on a car driving along a level road is perpendicular to the motion, so it does zero work; so does the string's tension on a ball moving in a circle. Check: find the angle between each force and the displacement before you multiply.
